title: some young buyers renting investing beats buying home 2026 09 10
text:
For Lydia Paternoster, investing what would be her first home deposit into the stock market is a conscious effort — one she believes will be a worthwhile path to financial stability.
“Being able to have more of my dream home rather than getting a starter home is definitely the approach that I'm taking,” she says.
The 25-year-old content creator and former accountant is constantly asking herself how much more money she can make by investing in the stock market — all while keeping her living costs low. If Paternoster bought the home she can afford where she lives in Texas, it would cost her thousands of dollars a year in mortgage payments and maintenance. “That's additional money every single year I could be investing,” she says.
Not to mention the perks of liquidity when it comes to investing. With a home, it could take a long time to sell. “I do like the security of being able to have access to the money when I want,” she says.
Paternoster has been investing since age 19. She now puts around $2,000 a month toward her investments from her monthly $8,000 salary. Being super consistent — even if just $100 or $50 a month — really made a difference over the years, she says, noting that she now has over $100,000 invested in a diverse portfolio of U.S. stocks, index funds and exchange-traded funds.
The ultimate goal for Paternoster is to front-load her savings and investments to the point where they can grow to cover her retirement needs without further contribution.“Even if it's just a couple of years of not owning a home, it will make such a difference in 20, 30, 40 years,” she says.
The Wider Trend
Young adults are less likely than older adults to say buying a home is a “very good” investment, according to a 2026 Pew Research Center survey, which found that just 37% of renter households younger than 40 can afford the monthly cost of owning a home in 2024, down from 56% in 2019.
Chad Chubb, the lead advisor and founder of WealthKeel, a financial planning firm, says his young clients are increasingly prioritizing investing over home ownership. “Home prices have climbed faster than wages in most metro areas, so the down payment and monthly payment math looks very different than it did 10 years ago,” he says. “Mortgage rates are also higher than the historic lows many people remember, which raises the cost of financing a home significantly.”
As young professionals watch their retirement and investment accounts compound, many are asking: Does it make more sense to keep that money working in the market, or tie it up in a down payment and a mortgage?
For those like Paternoster, the answer is to keep renting for a few more years while investing aggressively, then buy once income and life plans align.
Key Takeaways
Renting isn’t a financial loss — it’s a wealth-building choice. For people who value mobility or can invest the difference between rent and ownership costs, it can accelerate other financial goals.
Start investing early. Consistency matters more than a large starting balance. Investing $50 or $100 regularly can build momentum and benefit from long-term compounding.
Protect your financial foundation first. Do not sacrifice an emergency fund, retirement contributions or high-interest debt repayment just to assemble a down payment. Homeownership can build equity, but it also comes with taxes, insurance, maintenance and selling costs.
